reconcile.note: Clarke identifies the Bible's several Shebas as distinct men who share a name, rather than one figure with three conflicting fathers.

discrepancy.note: Colenso (quoting Delitzsch) calls Sheba's three genealogies irreconcilable; Wellhausen treats such clashes as typical of the Table of Nations' ethnographic genealogies.

quotes.text: It is impossible for us to keep asunder the Cushite Sheba, x.7, the Joktanite Sheba, x.28, and the Abrahamite Sheba, xxv.3.
quotes.attr: John William Colenso (d. 1883), The Pentateuch and Book of Joshua Critically Examined, Vol. IV (1863), quoting Franz Delitzsch, on the three genealogies of Sheba in Genesis 10 and 25.

quotes.text: Nor are apparent contradictions wanting in the ethnographic genealogy. Ishmael, Edom, and the Cainite tribes first mentioned, come into mutual contact in different ways, which may be quite naturally explained from different views and arrangements of their mutual relationships.
quotes.attr: Julius Wellhausen (d. 1918), Prolegomena to the History of Israel (1885), on the Table of Nations' ethnographic genealogies, of which Sheba's three fathers are one instance.

sides.snippet: The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.
sides.verseText: The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabteca. The sons of Raamah: Sheba and Dedan.

sides.snippet: Jokshan became the father of Sheba, and Dedan.
sides.verseText: Jokshan became the father of Sheba, and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.
